analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(1)(a): “Personal data shall be: (a) processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject (‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’);”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39: Processing should be lawful and fair and transparent to natural persons; information should be easily accessible and easy to understand, and clear and plain language should be used; individuals should be made aware of risks, rules, safeguards and rights.

relevant_clauses.text: “Ada Health GmbH (HRB 189710), Neue Grünstraße 17, 10179 Berlin, Germany being the data controller (as defined under Article 4(7) GDPR) of all processing activities in connection with the Services.”
“Our data protection officer can be contacted at [dpo@ada.com](mailto:dpo@ada.com).”

“Please read this Privacy Policy carefully to understand the types of data we collect from you, how we use it, the circumstances under which we will share it with third parties, and your rights in relation to your personal data.”

“In order to use our Symptom Assessment and other health related features, you have to consent to Ada analyzing the personal health data you voluntarily share in order to be provided with an assessment and health advice.”

“The information that we may ask you to provide includes, but is not limited to, your name, gender, date of birth, email address, phone number, symptoms of your illness... medical history... allergies...”
“3. Which personal data we may collect and process, why and for how long” (each activity lists “Types of data”, “Purpose of processing”, “Use justification”, “Storage duration”).
“Use justification: Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)GDPR)... We do not use the data collected for the purpose of identifying you.”
“Use justification: Contract performance (Article 6(1)(b)GDPR / Consent (Article9(2)(a) GDPR) for the processing of your health data.”
“No data will be shared with any third party without your specific consent.”

“you are not subject to a decision that is based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects... While your symptom assessment report is the result of automated processing, it is only intended for your information...”

“Limited data may... be processed by sub-processors operating outside of the European Economic Area (“EEA”)... as long as the additional requirements of Article 44 et seq. GDPR... are met... Your health data and other sensitive data will always stay in the EU.”
“Ada does not share your data for third-party commercial interests without your explicit consent.”
“Under GDPR you have various rights in relation to your personal data... All of these rights can be exercised by contacting us...”
“Right to withdraw consent... Right to object... Right to be informed... Right to erasure... Right to restriction... Right to data portability... Right to Rectification... Right to complain...”

analysis.justification: The policy identifies the controller and DPO and then explains, for each processing activity, the data types, purposes, legal basis (including Art. 9 bases for health data) and retention, which supports Article 5(1)(a)’s transparency and lawfulness requirements. It also discloses key safeguards and recipient categories (processors, third-country transfers, and consent-based sharing), enabling users to understand “rules, safeguards and rights” as Recital 39 expects. While the policy is long, it generally uses structured, intelligible explanations and provides contact points and a full rights section, aligning with Recital 39’s requirement for accessible information in clear language.

analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(1)(b): “Personal data shall be: (b) collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes; further processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes shall, in accordance with Article 89(1), not be considered to be incompatible with the initial purposes (‘purpose limitation’);”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39: The specific purposes for which personal data are processed should be explicit and legitimate and determined at the time of collection.

relevant_clauses.text: “This Privacy Policy describes our data processing when using the App, Ada Assess, the Website... Where certain processing activities relate only to a specific product this will be clearly indicated.”
“3. Which personal data we may collect and process, why and for how long” (each activity states “Purpose of processing”).
“we process your data including your health data to provide you with the requested functionality... identify and suggest possible causes... present options to address the identified causes...”

“For the avoidance of doubt, your data will only be processed to identify research projects you might be suitable for and invite you to them... Only when you specifically agree... will we use your personal data for those research projects or share it with our research partners.”
“We process pseudonymized data to carry out aggregate statistics...”
“We process pseudonymized data for public health purposes... We may share... summarized statistics... always on an irreversibly anonymized basis.”
“Post-market surveillance and medical safety... necessary to systematically monitor their quality, performance and safety...”
“Direct marketing... send you direct marketing... Those messages will not contain any health information about you.”

“If your personal data is used for more than one purpose, we will retain it until the purpose with the longest period expires, but we will stop using it for the purpose with the shorter period as soon as the shorter period expires (to comply with the purpose limitation principle).”
“Your data will not be used for any other purpose during that time.”

analysis.justification: The policy specifies purposes per processing context (e.g., symptom assessment, post-market surveillance, marketing, statistics, public health) and presents them alongside the relevant data categories at the point the processing is described, satisfying Article 5(1)(b)’s requirement for specified and explicit purposes. It also constrains secondary uses by requiring separate consent for research participation and by describing statistical/public-health uses as pseudonymized with outputs shared only in anonymized form, which is consistent with Article 5(1)(b)’s research/statistics compatibility logic and Recital 39’s emphasis on explicit purposes at collection. The retention section additionally commits to ceasing use for the shorter-purpose once that purpose ends, reinforcing purpose-bound processing.

analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(1)(c): “Personal data shall be: (c) adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’);”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39: Personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes; data should be processed only if the purpose cannot reasonably be fulfilled by other means.

relevant_clauses.text: “most functionalities rely on information about yourself and specifically your health. Without providing this information you might not be able to use those functionalities...”
“health insurance (optional), general data about your health (optional)...”
“We do not use the data collected for the purpose of identifying you.”
“although we will not use it to identify you, we may collect... Usage data... Analytics data...”
“Depending on the specific technical setup we might not be able to connect this account directly to you.”
“Before we share any data with Tableau, we remove all information that directly identifies you.”
“We only use pseudonymized usage data... We will never share your personal health information with advertisers...”
“We use a limited set of usage data (which does not include personal health data) to track your page interaction...”
“The data collected in the context is not used to link any usage profile with your personal data... Under no circumstances will we use the collected data to determine your identity.”
“for the validation of such capabilities we only use anonymized real world user data such as anonymized past assessment data...”
“We will hold your personal data... always in compliance with the data minimization principle.”

analysis.justification: The policy contains multiple minimisation controls (optional fields, “limited set” for marketing analytics, commitments not to identify users from certain technical datasets, and pseudonymization/anonymization for statistics and AI validation), which supports Article 5(1)(c) and Recital 39’s “limited to what is necessary” standard. However, several processing descriptions enumerate broad technical/behavioral datasets (e.g., detailed clickstream/interaction data and extensive device identifiers) without clearly demonstrating necessity or explaining why less intrusive data would not reasonably fulfil the same purposes, which Recital 39 expects. As a result, the minimisation rationale is strong in some areas (health-data secondary uses) but less substantiated for web/app analytics and monitoring.

analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(1)(d): “Personal data shall be: (d) accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate, having regard to the purposes for which they are processed, are erased or rectified without delay (‘accuracy’);”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39: Every reasonable step should be taken to ensure that personal data which are inaccurate are rectified or deleted.

relevant_clauses.text: “When you update information such as height and weight in your profile, we will keep the previous entries to allow you to track its development.”
“This can be the case, for example, if you contest the accuracy of the personal data... the restriction of processing lasts for a period that enables us to verify the accuracy...”
“Right to Rectification... you have the right to receive from us, without undue delay, the rectification of inaccuracies in your personal data and completion of incomplete personal data.”
“Verification: in order to verify your request, we will take reasonable steps...”

analysis.justification: The policy expressly provides a right to rectification “without undue delay” and describes mechanisms to restrict processing when accuracy is contested, which directly supports Article 5(1)(d)’s rectification/erasure expectation. This matches Recital 39’s requirement to take reasonable steps to ensure inaccurate data are rectified or deleted. The profile update feature also indicates ongoing data maintenance (and historical tracking) while still enabling correction via the rights process.

analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(1)(e): “Personal data shall be: (e) kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed; personal data may be stored for longer periods insofar as the personal data will be processed solely for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes in accordance with Article 89(1) subject to implementation of the appropriate technical and organisational measures required by this Regulation in order to safeguard the rights and freedoms of the data subject (‘storage limitation’);”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39: The period for which personal data are stored should be limited to a strict minimum; time limits should be established for erasure or for periodic review.

relevant_clauses.text: “Storage duration: Your data is removed after 15 days... Your data will be stored by Cloudflare for 6 months... If there is a security-relevant event, server log files are stored until...”
“We will then delete or irreversibly anonymize your case data... within 1 month.”
“We will delete the data latest within 45 days.”
“The data we process for the purpose of tracking is removed latest within 45 days.”
“Your data is removed after 60 days, unless a security-relevant event occurs...”
“After termination of the account, we will retain your data for up to seven years in secured form...”
“We will hold your personal data for as long as it is necessary or required by law or by any relevant regulatory body...”
“If your personal data is used for more than one purpose, we will retain it until the purpose with the longest period expires, but we will stop using it for the purpose with the shorter period...”
“We will retain Post-Market-Surveillance data (incl. health data) in accordance with our storage obligations according to the medical device law.”
“We will retain data (incl. health data) in relation to your use of our Services for up to seven years... for the purposes of establishing, exercising or defending against legal claims.”
“If the processing of your personal data is no longer necessary for any purpose it is either irreversibly anonymized... or securely erased.”

analysis.justification: The policy defines concrete retention periods for many data categories (e.g., 15 days for certain logs, 45/60 days for analytics/monitoring, 1 month for deletion/anonymization of case data), which supports Article 5(1)(e) and Recital 39’s “time limits” expectation. However, several key retention statements remain open-ended (e.g., “until no longer necessary” for post-market surveillance and security measures, and “as long as necessary” language in Section 7) without clear periodic review criteria or maximum caps beyond some contexts, weakening the “strict minimum” framing required by Recital 39. Longer retention for legal claims (up to seven years) is purpose-bounded and access-restricted, but the policy could better justify why that duration is necessary across all cases.

analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(1)(f): “Personal data shall be: (f) processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (‘integrity and confidentiality’).”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39: Processing should ensure appropriate security and confidentiality, including preventing unauthorised access, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.

relevant_clauses.text: “Ada implements a variety of technical and organisational measures to ensure that your data is adequately protected... required by law in Art. 32 GDPR and is also needed for the ISO 27001 certification...”
“Ada also runs bug bounty programs... we conclude a data processing agreement with all third parties involved in accordance with Art. 28 GDPR.”
“Sensitive information between your browser and our Website is transferred in encrypted form using Transport Layer Security (“TLS”).”
“We restrict access to your personal data to the persons who need to use it for the relevant purpose(s), always in compliance with the integrity and confidentiality principle.”

“we will encrypt and vault your data including your health information... Your data can only be accessed by limited personal subject to a procedure that involves approval by our Data Processing Officer.”
“We use technical service providers... who act as our processors based on data processing agreements as required by Art. 28 GDPR.”
“analyze the system security and stability...”; “to offer secure and functional services and to prevent misuse.”

analysis.justification: The policy describes concrete organisational and technical security measures (Art. 32-driven measures, ISO 27001 alignment, TLS encryption in transit, access restriction on a need-to-know basis, and encryption/vaulting for litigation retention), which addresses Article 5(1)(f)’s requirement for appropriate security against unauthorised access and loss. It also ties processor handling to Art. 28 DPAs and limits access via approval procedures, supporting confidentiality controls consistent with Recital 39’s emphasis on secure processing. While detailed implementation specifics are not exhaustively listed, the policy provides a credible security framework and safeguards proportional to health-data sensitivity.

analysis.article_5_text: Article 5(2): “The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1 (‘accountability’).”
analysis.recital_39_reference: Recital 39 is silent on Article 5(2); accountability is assessed directly under Article 5(2)’s requirement to take responsibility for and be able to demonstrate compliance with Article 5(1).

relevant_clauses.text: “Ada Health GmbH... being the data controller... of all processing activities in connection with the Services.”
“Our data protection officer can be contacted at [dpo@ada.com](mailto:dpo@ada.com).”
“The implementation of these security measures is expressly required by law in Art. 32 GDPR and is also needed for the ISO 27001 certification...”
“processors based on data processing agreements as required by Art. 28 GDPR.”
“Please contact us if you would like further details on the specific safeguards applied to the export of your personal data outside the EEA.”
“Specific storage periods for the respective processing activities are detailed in section 3 above.”
“approval by our Data Processing Officer” (access-gating for vaulted litigation data).

analysis.justification: The policy evidences some accountability mechanisms—identifying the controller and DPO, describing processor DPAs (Art. 28), referencing Art. 32 security measures and ISO 27001, and providing structured records of purposes/legal bases/retention in Section 3—supporting responsibility for compliance. However, Article 5(2) also requires demonstrability, and the policy does not clearly commit to (or describe) core demonstrability tools such as maintaining records of processing, DPIAs for high-risk health processing, internal audits, or governance controls beyond general statements. As written, it shows partial but not complete evidence that Ada can systematically demonstrate compliance with all Article 5(1) principles.
